issues.legal_issue: The compensation factors in the general land-acquisition framework apply to compulsory acquisitions under the national-highway framework despite the latter framework’s provisions on compensation.
material_facts: The land was compulsorily acquired for a highway, and compensation was determined through statutory arbitration rather than arbitration under a contract.

The national-highway enactment was included in the schedule to the 2013 land-acquisition legislation, and a government order extended that legislation’s compensation benefits to acquisitions under the scheduled enactments.
issues.conclusion: The compensation-determination factors in Sections 26 to 28 of the Right to Fair Compensation and Transparency in Land Acquisition, Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 apply to acquisitions under the National Highways Act, notwithstanding Sections 3J and 3G(7)(a) of that Act.
issues.legal_principle: The 2015 Removal of Difficulties Order extended the compensation provisions of the 2013 Act to the enactments listed in its Fourth Schedule. Applying different compensation standards to similarly situated landowners based only on the acquisition enactment would offend Article 14. Union of India v. Tarsem Singh, (2019) 9 SCC 304, held Section 3J unconstitutional concerning solatium and interest; the Court applied the same equality reasoning to all aspects of compensation determination. Articles 300A and 31A also require deprivation of property under authority of law with compensation. Sections 26 to 28 of the 2013 Act therefore guide compensation determination alongside Section 3G(7)(a) of the National Highways Act.

predicates.compulsory_land_acquisition: Land was compulsorily taken from an owner for a public purpose.
predicates.statutory_compensation_arbitration: A statutory arbitration process was used to determine compensation rather than arbitration under a contract.
predicates.acquisition_framework_receives_extended_: The acquisition framework was among those to which the general land-acquisition compensation benefits had been extended.

issues.definition: When land is compulsorily acquired through statutory compensation arbitration under a framework receiving the extended benefits, the general land-acquisition compensation factors apply.

issues.legal_issue: A registration-guideline value published after the acquisition notification may be considered where the revision process began before that notification and the revised value reflects a process close in time to the acquisition.
material_facts: The acquisition notification preceded the revised registration-guideline notification.
The process to revise the guideline values had begun before the acquisition notification, and the revision was published within a relatively short period after the earlier guideline values.
The final acquisition notification and the later award notice followed the revised guideline notification.
The earlier guideline used by the acquiring authority treated the acquired lands as agricultural, although the lands had been converted to non-agricultural uses.
issues.conclusion: In these circumstances, reliance on the later guideline notification was not, merely because it post-dated the acquisition notification, patent illegality.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3G(7)(a) of the National Highways Act fixes the acquisition-notification date as the relevant date for market value. Ordinarily, valuation evidence should reflect values before that date, but the valuation exercise is fact-specific and admits no rigid formula. Section 26(1)(a) of the 2013 Act expressly permits use of the value specified for registration under the stamp legislation. Where the guideline revision process began before acquisition and the revised notification closely followed the earlier guideline, the revised value may reflect the escalation that could otherwise have been accounted for. The Court distinguished the observations in National Highways Authority of India v. M. Hakeem, (2021) 9 SCC 1, because they were not based on the statutory language of Section 26(1)(a).

predicates.statutory_compensation_arbitration: Compensation for compulsorily acquired land was determined through statutory arbitration.
predicates.revised_guideline_published_after_acquis: The relevant registration-guideline value was published after the acquisition notice.
predicates.guideline_revision_started_before_acquis: The administrative process to revise the guideline value began before the acquisition notice.
predicates.revised_guideline_reflects_nearby_market: The revised guideline followed the earlier guideline closely enough to reflect a contemporaneous revision in market values.

issues.definition: A later-published guideline is not, by timing alone, patent illegality when its revision began before the acquisition notice and it reflects a nearby market revision.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitrator determining compensation cannot apply the value of a separate layout to acquired land without evidence supporting comparability, an opportunity for the opposing party to respond, and reasons for the comparison.
material_facts: The arbitrator relied on a published guideline notification that stated one value for the acquired lands’ survey numbers and a higher value for separate residential layouts.
The claimants’ pleadings did not identify the guideline notification or plead a comparison with those layouts, and the record did not establish that the acquired lands were comparable to them.
The arbitrator applied the layout value without adequately explaining why it was appropriate, and the acquiring authority lacked sufficient opportunity to controvert the material or the comparison.
issues.conclusion: The method of applying the separate layout values without sufficient opportunity and reasons amounted to patent illegality, and the awards could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 18 and 24(3) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 require a full opportunity to present a case and communication of material supplied to or relied on by the tribunal. Sections 28(2) and 31(3) require a fair process and a reasoned award. Under Section 34(2A), patent illegality includes an award based on material not properly put to the parties or a conclusion lacking sufficient reasons on a material comparison. Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd. v. NHAI, (2019) 15 SCC 131, and Delhi Airport Metro Express (P) Ltd. v. DMRC, (2022) 1 SCC 131, explain that reliance on material not shared with a party and findings based on no evidence or ignoring vital evidence can constitute patent illegality. Dyna Technologies (P) Ltd. v. Crompton Greaves Ltd., (2019) 20 SCC 1, explains the requirement for intelligible and adequate reasoning.

predicates.compensation_arbitration: An arbitrator determined compensation for compulsorily acquired land.
predicates.separate_property_value_used_for_acquire: The arbitrator applied a value stated for a distinct property or layout to the acquired land.
predicates.comparability_not_supported_by_evidence: The record did not contain evidence establishing that the distinct property was comparable to the acquired land.
predicates.opposing_party_lacked_fair_opportunity_t: The opposing party did not have a fair opportunity to address the material or the proposed comparison.

issues.definition: When an arbitrator uses a separate property’s value without evidentiary support for comparability and without a fair opportunity for response, the award may be set aside for reconsideration.

issues.legal_issue: An arbitrator cannot combine the base value from one guideline notification with an enhancement instruction from a different notification to determine compensation.
material_facts: The acquired land was industrial land, and the earlier guideline notification relied on by the arbitrator did not specify a value for industrial plots.
The arbitrator used the earlier notification’s value as the base and relied on a later notification’s special instruction to add an amount for industrial use.
The award did not resolve the applicable valuation method by considering the relevant instructions in the earlier notification or assigning reasons for the combined method.
issues.conclusion: Using the base value from one notification and the enhancement instruction from another was a material irregularity and patent illegality; the award had to be set aside for reconsideration.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34(2A) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 permits interference for patent illegality going to the root of the award, but does not allow the reviewing court to reappreciate evidence or substitute its own valuation. Sections 28(2) and 31(3) require a fair determination supported by reasons. Associate Builders v. Delhi Development Authority, (2015) 3 SCC 49, Ssangyong Engineering & Construction Co. Ltd. v. NHAI, (2019) 15 SCC 131, and Delhi Airport Metro Express (P) Ltd. v. DMRC, (2022) 1 SCC 131, describe the limits of review and the patent-illegality standard.

predicates.industrial_land_compensation_arbitration: An arbitrator determined compensation for acquired industrial land.
predicates.base_value_taken_from_one_guideline: The arbitrator used one guideline notification to establish the base value.
predicates.enhancement_instruction_taken_from_anoth: The arbitrator used a separate guideline notification to calculate an enhancement to that base value.

issues.definition: When compensation for industrial land is calculated using a base value from one guideline and an enhancement from another, the combined method requires reconsideration.

issues.legal_issue: The initial compensation determination by the acquiring authority remains an offer and may be reassessed by the statutory arbitrator using additional relevant material without first finding an error in that determination.
material_facts: The acquiring authority had determined compensation after considering sale transactions and an earlier registration guideline.
The landowners challenged that amount in statutory arbitration and relied on additional material relevant to fair compensation.
The acquiring authority argued that its determination should not be disturbed unless shown to be erroneous.
issues.conclusion: The acquiring authority’s determination remains an offer of compensation; the arbitrator may consider additional material that assists in determining just and fair compensation without first establishing an error in the initial determination.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3G(5) of the National Highways Act permits either party dissatisfied with the competent authority’s determination to seek statutory arbitration. The determination does not acquire the status of a judicially considered order merely because the acquiring authority considered evidence or either party may challenge it. Sections 26 and 28 of the 2013 Act guide the arbitrator’s determination of fair compensation. Union of India v. Tarsem Singh, (2019) 9 SCC 304, was considered regarding the changed acquisition process, but the change in procedure did not transform the competent authority’s determination into a judicial decision.

predicates.statutory_compensation_arbitration: A party challenged a compensation determination through statutory arbitration.
predicates.initial_compensation_determined_by_acqui: The acquiring authority made an initial determination of compensation for the acquired land.
predicates.relevant_additional_material_presented: Additional material relevant to determining fair compensation was presented to the arbitrator.

issues.definition: When statutory arbitration follows an initial compensation determination and relevant additional material is presented, the arbitrator may reassess compensation without first finding the initial determination erroneous.

issues.legal_issue: A court reviewing a statutory compensation award cannot alter the compensation amount but may set aside the award and remit the matter for a reasoned reconsideration where the award has a reviewable defect.
material_facts: The challenges arose under the review and appeal provisions governing arbitral awards.
The awards used valuation methods that lacked adequate evidentiary support or reasons, or combined guideline values from different notifications.
The reviewing courts had upheld the awards, and the Supreme Court found defects requiring further consideration by the arbitrators.
issues.conclusion: The awards and the decisions upholding them were set aside, and the matters were remanded to the arbitrators; the reviewing court could not itself modify the compensation.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 34 and 37 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 do not confer appellate power to modify or vary an award. Where a defect is established, the available course is to set aside the award; Section 34(4) may be used to give the tribunal an opportunity to address a curable defect. National Highways Authority of India v. M. Hakeem, (2021) 9 SCC 1, holds that the limited remedy is setting aside or remitting in the circumstances permitted by the Act, not modifying the award. Dyna Technologies (P) Ltd. v. Crompton Greaves Ltd., (2019) 20 SCC 1, addresses the use of Section 34(4) to cure defects in reasoning.

predicates.challenge_to_arbitral_award: A party challenged an arbitral award through the statutory court-review process.
predicates.reviewable_award_defect: The award contained a defect that permits judicial intervention, such as a failure of fair opportunity or adequate reasons.
predicates.compensation_requires_further_arbitral_d: Further assessment by the arbitrator is needed to determine compensation.

issues.definition: When a reviewable defect requires further arbitral assessment, the court may set aside and remit the award but may not itself change the compensation.
